item.title: [NBC Sports] Were we wrong about Yankees rookie outfielder Spencer Jones?
item.dc:creator: Eric Samulski
item.description: When Yankees’ outfielder Spencer Jones made his MLB debut back in May, many people, including myself, were skeptical that his approach would work at the MLB level. While he had succeeded in the minors, he was older than most of his opponents and had displayed real issues with contact and strikeouts. It didn’t seem like a profile that would translate well and, early on, that was proven to be correct. In his first 82 plate appearances, Jones hit .233 with a 41.5% strikeout rate, a 21% swinging str
item.content:encoded:
When Yankees’ outfielder Spencer Jones made his MLB debut back in May, many people, including myself, were skeptical that his approach would work at the MLB level. While he had succeeded in the minors, he was older than most of his opponents and had displayed real issues with contact and strikeouts. It didn’t seem like a profile that would translate well and, early on, that was proven to be correct.
In his first 82 plate appearances, Jones hit .233 with a 41.5% strikeout rate, a 21% swinging strike rate, and well below-average contact rates and zone contact rates. The Yankees demoted him to Triple-A at the beginning of July, and it seemed like he may not be part of the team’s plans moving forward.
Yet, since coming back up on July 22nd, Jones is hitting .261/.326/.472 with eight home runs, 30 RBI, and eight steals. That has come with a 33.5% strikeout rate and a 19.5% swinging strike rate, but also a 77% zone contact rate that is better than many expected him to produce. So is this sustainable? Can Jones keep producing at this level with his strikeout rates and swinging strike rates as elevated as they are?
To answer that question, I not only went to the data, but I watched the vast majority of his at-bats since July 22nd, thanks, in huge part, to my buddy Nick Pollack, who gave me access to a pitcher database where you can watch specific at-bats. We don’t have to tell Nick that I watched it for a hitter instead of a pitcher. Regardless, this article is now a combination of what the data and my own eyes tell me about whether or not my Spencer Jones skepticism was off base and if he can be a true difference-maker for the Yankees during his career.
The Results Don’t Lie - He Hits the Ball Incredibly Hard
We have to start with the results because if they weren’t what they are, nobody would be asking this question. We already talked about Jones’ stat line and his contact rate since returning to the Yankees’ roster. We should also note that he has a 19.4% barrel rate, 51.5% hard-hit rate, and 77 mph bat speed in his 179 plate appearances. All of that is beyond elite. No matter where he makes contact with the ball (except maybe up-and-in), he’s crushing it.
Despite also having a .362 BABIP over this stretch, Jones is not getting lucky, according to Statcast, which gives him a .266 xBA and a .520 xSLG. At bare minimum, it means that Jones’ performance is not obviously flukey based on batted ball data. His .362 BABIP may regress closer to the league average of .290 over this stretch, but the rest of the results aren’t screaming red flags. Which means we can start digging into the details with a slight lean towards an optimistic view on Jones.
Jones Crushes Fastballs But Can He Handle Other Pitches?
As you might expect from a player with Jones’ raw power, he handles fastballs, both four-seamers and sinkers, exceptionally well. Heading into Wednesday’s game against the Twins, Jones had a .936 OPS since July 22nd against four-seamers, with a 96.0 mph average exit velocity, 22.7% barrel rate, and 54.5% hard-hit rate. That’s genuinely elite contact quality. His expected batting average against four-seamers was .426, which was notably higher than his .317 actual average, which supports that he has been hitting four-seamers as well as you could expect a hitter to.
In a much smaller sample size, Jones’ sinker results look even better, with a 1.103 OPS, 99 mph average exit velocity, and 66.7% hard-hit rate. Of course, he has only seen 67 sinkers, so we need to take that with a grain of salt, but it’s notable that both the fastball and sinker feature the lowest swinging strike rates for Jones among all of the pitches he has faced regularly (he didn’t face enough splitters for me to include the data).
| Pitch Type | Pitches Seen | BA | OPS | SwStr% | Avg Exit Velo | Hard-Hit% | Balls In Play | Expected BA (xBA) |
| Four-seam | 288 | 0.317 | 0.936 | 13.5% | 96.0 | 54.5% | 44 | 0.426 |
| Changeup | 103 | 0.160 | 0.512 | 31.1% | 89.8 | 41.7% | 12 | 0.398 |
| Slider | 90 | 0.227 | 0.655 | 25.6% | 94.1 | 46.2% | 13 | 0.402 |
| Sinker | 67 | 0.286 | 1.103 | 10.4% | 99.0 | 66.7% | 9 | 0.595 |
| Curveball | 49 | 0.100 | 0.200 | 26.5% | 88.3 | 50.0% | 6 | 0.304 |
| Sweeper | 34 | 0.625 | 1.625 | 17.6% | 88.7 | 42.9% | 7 | 0.433 |
As you can see from the pitch samples, again, before Wednesday’s game, Jones has seen four-seamers nearly three times as often as any other single pitch. That’s a curious decision from pitchers given the amount of damage he does against them, but that’s a conversation for another time.
We can also notice from the chart that Jones’ hard-hit rate is genuinely strong against all pitch types. However, the swinging strike rate gets significantly worse, particularly on changeups, where Jones has a 31.1% mark. Considering he has seen over 100 changeups, that is likely not a small-sample-size data error; Jones really struggles against changeups. Similarly, in a much smaller sample size, he has struggled to make contact with curveballs, but has hit them hard, so this all jives pretty cleanly with the idea that Jones has tons of power in his bat, but struggles to make consistent contact. If he were to start seeing far fewer four-seamers, how would he handle that?
Contact Rate and Swing Decisions Concerns
Earlier, I mentioned that Jones’ 77% zone contact rate over this stretch was far better than I expected him to produce. While that’s true, we also need to highlight that the MLB average zone contact rate over the same sample size is 87.1%. Similarly, his 19.5% swinging strike rate is well above the 10.8% league average, and his 64% contact rate overall is below the league average of 77.4%. No matter which way you slice it, Jones is far below the league average when it comes to his contact ability, even when he’s producing such elite results.
In fact, over this stretch, only Munetaka Murakami and Esmerlyn Valdez have a lower contact rate among the 168 qualified hitters in all of baseball. Jones ranks 166th out of 168 qualified hitters in contact rate despite his scorching results at the plate. Similarly, his 77% zone contact rate, which we lauded, ranks 161st out of 168 qualified hitters.
In particular, he seems to have a weakness up in the zone and particularly up-and-away. As you can see in the Statcast zone breakdowns below, Jones whiffs more at the top of the zone than anywhere else, and he produces poor batted ball results at the top of the zone. That might be why he sees so many fastballs, but if pitchers aren’t able to locate successfully up in the zone, Jones can punish pitches in the middle of the zone and also low. However, these charts seem to show some real weak points where pitchers could attack the rookie.
Some of Jones’ contact concerns come down to swing decisions. Jones has a chase rate of 37.9% over this stretch, which is the 39th-most among the same 168 qualified hitters. Jones also sees his chase rate climb as he gets deeper into the count. It’s 36.6% when he’s ahead in the count, 38.7% when he’s in an even count, and 40.2% when he’s behind in the count. All of that is compared to the league average chase rate over the same sample size of 33.2%. While it’s natural for hitters to expand the zone more to try and protect the plate in two-strike counts, we have to acknowledge that Jones expands the zone far more than average in all counts.
Part of that is aggression. He has a 53.7% swing rate over this stretch that ranks 23rd among the same batch of qualified hitters. The league average swing rate is 47.6%. Yet, swinging more often makes sense for Jones. We’ve seen plenty of hitters with poor contact profiles swing more often because it gives them more chances to make contact and do damage. That aggression is not necessarily a negative for him so long as it results in early swing and misses that give him extra chances to hit and not weak contact that ends an at-bat.
That might also be why Jones gets even MORE aggressive with runners in scoring position, where his swing rate increases from 51.2% to 59.5%, and his chase rate climbs from 36.6% to 44.4%. When you pair that with the fact that his contact rate and swinging-strike rate are both also worse with runners in scoring position, you’d think Jones struggles there, but he actually entered Wednesday’s game with a .378 batting average and 1.158 OPS with runners in scoring position. That’s compared to a .211 average and .657 OPS with the bases empty. His aggression in those situations has potentially been the cause of his success.
This also isn’t luck. He may be getting overly aggressive with runners in scoring position and expanding the zone a lot, but when he puts the ball in play in these spots, he’s genuinely crushing it. He has three home runs in these situations, and all three were balls that were 104.6 mph or harder. He has singles that registered 105.9 mph, 102.2 mph, and 108.5 mph. In fact, he has only one poorly hit base hit with runners in scoring position over this whole sample, which was a 53.1 mph roller with a -28° launch angle that found a hole for a single.
So, yes, his contact rates and swing decisions are not good. But also, no, that has not been hurting his overall performance.
He Is Willing to Make Two-Strike Adjustments
Another factor that points towards Jones’ results being genuine is that he has shown the desire to change his approach in two-strike counts. That’s good because he gets into a lot of them. Since July 22nd, 60% of Jones’ plate appearances reach a two-strike count. The league average is 52.7%. We obviously mentioned his aggression earlier on in this article, and we know that Jones swings and misses a lot, so it makes sense that he would get behind in the count often.
Yet, when his aggression works for him, it works in impressive ways.
In the 40% of plate appearances where Jones avoids a two-strike count, he has hit .460 with a 1.341 OPS and a 50.8% hard-hit rate. Now, we need to note that a 1.341 OPS in 63 at-bats is an extreme number that we should expect to come back down to earth as the sample grows. That’s not because Jones is bad, but because numbers this high rarely hold at that level over a larger sample size.
Now, when Jones does get into two-strike counts, his bat speed, swing length, and swing tilt are all essentially unchanged, which means he’s not making any glaring mechanical changes depending on the count. However, his attack angle, which measures the vertical angle of the sweet spot of the bat when it passes through the contact point, is over two degrees flatter in two-strike counts. That may be a small sample size fluke, but it also may be evidence that Jones is trying to create a flatter bat path when he gets behind in the count.
Another data point that supports that notion is that Jones’ best contact rate comes in two-strike counts. Now, it’s still just 71.3%, and his swinging strike rate in two-strike counts remains 16%, but those are noticeable improvements from what he’s doing in other counts. This supports the idea that he is tightening up his swing and focusing on making contact in these situations. That contact has produced just a .481 OPS, which is a huge gap of about .860 points between his two-strike and non-two-strike OPS; however, we can’t drag a guy for not making enough contact and then also drag him when he changes his swing to protect the plate and make more contact. It’s clear that Jones has the mature understanding that he needs to change his approach with two strikes, and that points to continued development from him in the future.
Is On the Extreme End of a Common Profile
In order to see which hitters Jones most closely resembles, I sorted by hitters who were in both the top quartile in swinging strike rate (negatively), zone contact rate (negatively), and the top quartile in hard-hit rate (positively). I found 33 hitters who have similar types of profiles to Spencer Jones. A lot of them are names you’d likely have imagined, and even after I removed a few of them because they either didn’t hit the ball hard enough or made too much contact in the zone, we had an intriguing list to compare to.
| Player | SwStr% | Hard-Hit% | Zone Contact% |
| Esmerlyn Valdez | 14.9% | 49.3% | 71.3% |
| Munetaka Murakami | 15.9% | 57.1% | 71.3% |
| Luke Raley | 20.6% | 47.1% | 76.9% |
| Spencer Jones | 19.5% | 54.3% | 77.0% |
| Nick Kurtz | 14.1% | 57.3% | 77.5% |
| Garrett Mitchell | 14.5% | 53.1% | 80.0% |
| Griffin Conine | 16.9% | 49.7% | 80.1% |
| Oneil Cruz | 14.5% | 55.4% | 80.2% |
| Kyle Stowers | 17.5% | 56.5% | 82.1% |
| Kyle Schwarber | 13.3% | 49.9% | 82.3% |
| Jordan Walker | 15.3% | 48.9% | 82.6% |
| Jake Burger | 16.5% | 46.3% | 82.8% |
| Corey Seager | 14.9% | 48.4% | 84.3% |
| Henry Bolte | 15.1% | 47.8% | 85.3% |
| Heliot Ramos | 13.2% | 50.4% | 86.2% |
| Jac Caglianone | 14.9% | 54.5% | 87.2% |
As you can see, even from this list of outliers, Jones is an outlier himself. He has the 4th-lowest zone contact rate (77%) in the entire 33-player group, basically tied with Luke Raley. Only Esmerlyn Valdez and Munetaka Murakami have been worse among this group. Both of those two hitters had better swinging-strike rates than Jones, whose swinging strike rate is second-highest on this list, trailing only Raley. Of course, on the flip side, only five hitters in the 33-hitter sample had a higher hard-hit rate than Jones, which puts him as a positive outlier too. All of which is to say that Jones, even during his recent hot streak, has proven to swing and miss an extreme amount, both overall and in the zone, but also hit the ball incredibly hard when he does make contact.
I found the comparisons to Esmerlyn Valdez and Munetaka Murakami to be interesting because both have proven to be incredibly streaky this season.
In his first 74 games of the season, Murakami hit .244/.382/.553 with 24 home runs and 51 RBI. That came with a 20.1% barrel rate and 60.4% hard-hit rate. He was among the most elite power hitters in the game. That’s also a 344 plate appearance sample, so almost double Jones’ 179 plate appearances. Murakami’s 16.3% swinging strike rate was better than Jones’ mark by over 3%; however, Murakami had a far worse 70.3% zone contact rate and a slightly worse 60.4% contact rate.
It appears that his hamstring injury, or poor contact rates, caught up with Murakami, who has hit .131/.277/.301 with seven home runs and a 42% strikeout rate in 184 plate appearances since August 1st. His zone contact rate is an identical 70.4% over that stretch, and his contact rate fell to 59.2%. It’s unlikely that Jones would experience that kind of regression since his zone contact issues are not as pronounced as Murakami’s.
The same could maybe be said for Valdez, who was also called back up after a rough first MLB sample size, and hit .310/.406/.716 with 12 home runs and 32 RBI in his first 138 plate appearances from June 22nd on. Remember that this sample size for Jones is 179 plate appearances, so Valdez wasn’t as hot for as long, but it’s a closer gap than Murakami. Valdez also, like Murakami, scorched the ball with a 24.7% barrel rate and 51% hard-hit rate, but also posted a 73% zone contact rate and 66% contact rate overall. Interestingly, that means Valdez had a better swinging strike rate and overall contact rate than Jones over his sample size; however, Valdez also had more issues with contact in the zone.
In 123 plate appearances since August 1st, Valdez has hit .178/.317/.317 with three home runs and a 41.5% strikeout rate. Even though his profile is more similar to Jones’ than Murakami’s, I still don’t think it’s quite a fair comparison because Jones has had better zone contact rates, so he may not have regression hit him as hard as those two players did.
So who does Jones most closely resemble?
That hard truth is that the answer is really “Nobody.” Jones combines three separate extremes at the same time, which appears to be rare when you look at the hitters on this list. Most of these hitters, who are already elite power hitters with some contact concerns, have two extreme outcomes but are closer to league average in a third. For example, Nick Kurtz has a near-identical zone contact rate to Jones and only slightly better hard-hit rates, but a significantly better swinging strike rate. Kyle Stowers has a hard-hit rate that resembles Jones’ and also has an elevated swinging strike rate, but both of those marks are better than Jones’, and Stowers also has a 5% better zone contact rate.
Jones’ basic archetype of being a high-whiff, big-power hitter isn’t rare, but when factoring in zone contact, he struggles to make contact on pitches he should be able to handle at a rate that’s similar to almost no other hitter who also hits the ball this hard. Your closest comparison might be Griffin Conine or maybe Luke Raley with more pop and athleticism (meaning, he can actually play defense).
We need to be clear that this isn’t who Jones WILL BE. He’s 25 years old, so there is a world where he continues to improve and adjust to MLB pitching and comes closer to an Oneil Cruz type of profile; although, even that would require a 5% decrease in swinging strike rate. He should also note that Cruz has a career slash line of .241/.320/.436, so even if we’re saying the contact profile for Jones could grow into becoming more than Cruz, that would likely still result in a far lower batting average over a full season.
Final Takeaway
At the end of the day, Spencer Jones is a truly unique player. We’ve really yet to see somebody who truly resembles his profile as closely as we’d like. However, we can say that he’s clearly better than I, and many others, thought he’d be at the MLB level. That needs to be said directly and outright if we’re being honest in our takeaways from this research. I thought his contact profile would be so poor that he would rarely be able to make enough useful contact to be an MLB regular. I underestimated the quality of contact that he is able to make when he does square up the ball.
However, I do maintain my belief that contact rate wins out in the end. I’ve just seen it too many times over all my years playing, watching, and writing about baseball. It’s nearly impossible for a player to maintain consistent, year-after-year production with bottom-tier contact rates. Major League pitchers are simply too good, and they find a way to exploit it.
That being said, I think it’s fair to come away from this believing that Jones is an MLB regular. He possesses good speed and a solid enough defensive profile that I think you can play him as one of your regular outfielders. He has also hit left-handers well enough in a small sample size that you may not need to force a strong-side platoon on him. However, I think there’s also a strong argument that we’re seeing the best stretch he’s going to have. Considering that stretch has a .261/.326/.472 slash line, we might see Jones settle in as a .240 type of hitter.
There are plenty of those types of hitters who are impactful MLB players: Oneil Cruz, Kyle Schwarber, Max Muncy, Hunter Goodman, etc. Jones will need to continue to make strides to get near that tier of player, but he’s showing that it may not be as impossible as I had believed. Although maybe still a little improbable.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yankees’ Aaron Judge Injury News Has To Wait
item.dc:creator: Billy Heyen
item.description: The schedule may have done the New York Yankees a tiny favor in regards to what happens next after Aaron Judge left Wednesday's game in Minnesota with an injury. The Yankees are off on Thursday before returning to action Friday, so it's a built-in rest day of sorts. It also means, though, that Yankees fans waiting for a quick turnaround on another Judge update may have to be patient. item.content:encoded:
The schedule may have done the New York Yankees a tiny favor in regards to what happens next after Aaron Judge left Wednesday's game in Minnesota with an injury.
The Yankees are off on Thursday before returning to action Friday, so it's a built-in rest day of sorts.
It also means, though, that Yankees fans waiting for a quick turnaround on another Judge update may have to be patient. There's less likelihood of additional news emerging on Thursday when the Yankees don't have a game to play.
The Yankees are on the road and won't play again until Friday night in Arizona against the Diamondbacks. That game will begin at what is 9:40 p.m. ET back in the Bronx.
Aaron Judge Injury: What Happened?
Judge was lifted for a pinch-hitter during the Yankees' 5-4 loss to the Twins on Wednesday.
Heliot Ramos entered to take that sixth-inning at bat in place of Judge.
Judge said after the game that he felt stiffness in his lower right leg in the first inning. He struck out in his first two at bats and played the field as well before the decision was made to get him out of the game.
"I tried to kind of play it off and see how long we could go, because these games are important down the stretch," Judge said after the game, via MLB.com. "But kind of talking it over, I thought it'd be the right move to come out, so I don't cost the team on the field or cost the team on the basepath."
MLB.com's Patrick Donnelly wrote after the game that Judge is going to receive "extensive treatment over the next 48 hours."
Judge added after the game that he couldn't pinpoint a specific moment that the injury may have occurred. He noted that the ramp up in his return from the rib injury that kept him out for more than three months might explain this — "Once you start ramping up again, things pop up, and that's where we've been," Judge said.
What's Next for Aaron Judge?
The Yankees aren't jumping to conclusions.
"We're not going to speculate one way or the other," manager Aaron Boone told reporters after Wednesday's game. "We'll just see how he responds."
It's not going to be an easy finishing run for the Yankees.
The three-game series in Arizona comes against a Diamondbacks team that has a fighting chance to claim the National League's final Wild Card spot, so they'll be playing hard.
Then beginning on Tuesday, Sept. 22, the Yankees play a four-game set (with a doubleheader on 9/22) against the Tampa Bay Rays that could determine in a big way who wins the AL East Division.
After that, the Yankees close the season at home with a three-game series against the Baltimore Orioles.
The Yankees have already clinched a playoff berth, so it's most important for them to have Judge in October. They'd also like him for the stretch run, though, if they can have him.
"Obviously he's a key figure of what we do," Boone said after Wednesday's game. "Hopefully we get it treated and knock it out and be a factor at some point."
Like HEAVY's content? Be sure to follow us.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Yankees' Aaron Judge Injury News Has To Wait appeared first on HEAVY.

item.title: [Pinstripes Nation] Lombard Se Lleva La Culpa, Pero La Derrota Por 5-4 De Los Yankees Ante Los Twins, Tras 13 Entradas, Tiene Muchos Culpables
item.dc:creator: Esteban Quiñones

item.content:encoded:
MINNEAPOLIS — Anthony Volpe bateó con tanta fuerza que perdió el equilibrio, convencido de que la pelota se había ido fuera. En cambio, rebotó contra el muro alto del centro-derecha, un doble de dos carreras que igualó el marcador para los Yankees con dos outs en la novena entrada. Durante un momento intenso y emocionante el miércoles, Nueva York parecía dispuesta a llevarse la barrida.
Lo que vino después fueron cuatro entradas más en las que el equipo llegaba hasta la puerta y se negaba a cruzarla. Los Yankees se pusieron por delante en la décima. Volvieron a hacerlo en la undécima. Llenaron las bases sin outs en la duodécima. Cada vez acababan con un empate o con una remontada desperdiciada.
Un viaje que debería haber acabado con una barrida acabó poniendo de manifiesto el único punto débil que un aspirante al título no puede permitirse arrastrar hasta octubre. No se trató de un colapso del bullpen ni de un rebote desafortunado. Fue la alineación de los Yankees la que no paraba de preparar la mesa, pero nunca se sentaba a comer.
La culpa final recayó en un novato que no se la merecía él solo.
Los Minnesota Twins vencieron a los Yankees por 5-4 en 13 entradas, poniendo fin a ese partido maratoniano con un sencillo de Victor Caratini en la primera base que rebotó en el montículo y se coló por debajo del guante de George Lombard Jr. en la segunda base. Con esta derrota, Nueva York queda con un balance de 88-64, a cuatro partidos de los Rays de Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana, a falta de 10 partidos por disputar. Los Yankees ya tienen asegurada su plaza en los playoffs, pero el título de la división y la exención de la primera ronda se les están escapando.
Una remontada que no llevó a ninguna parte
Nueva York había sumado cuatro hits en ocho entradas y perdía por 2-0, mientras que el lanzador diestro de los Twins, Zebby Matthews, había ponchado a ocho. Entonces llegó la novena entrada. Lombard conectó un sencillo, Paul Goldschmidt le siguió y el corredor suplente José Caballero preparó el terreno para Volpe.
Volpe impulsó las dos carreras, lo que le supuso al cerrador de los Twins, Yoendrys Gómez, su primer salvamento fallido del año y obligó a jugar entradas extras.
Ali Sánchez impulsó al corredor automático con un sencillo en la décima entrada, dando a los Yankees su primera ventaja. Luke Keaschall respondió con un sencillo que empató el partido ante David Bednar. Un fly de sacrificio de Caballero puso a Nueva York por delante en la undécima. Royce Lewis igualó el marcador. Dos ventajas, dos respuestas inmediatas.
La entrada que dará que hablar
La 12.ª es la entrada que los aficionados volverán a ver una y otra vez. Los Yankees llenaron las bases sin outs, la situación que debería haber sentenciado el partido. Pero no sacaron nada de ella.
Heliot Ramos, que bateaba en el turno de Aaron Judge, mandó una bola corta hacia el montículo. Travis Adams la convirtió en una doble jugada 1-2-3. Sánchez se fue con un strikeout, dejando a otros dos en base. Los Yankees acabaron con 7 de 30 con corredores en posición de anotar.
El juez se marcha y el ataque se queda con pocos jugadores
Judge se retiró en la sexta entrada por una contractura en la parte inferior de la pierna derecha que empezó a notar en la primera entrada. Falló dos veces y no volvió al campo, solo siete partidos después de una ausencia de 99 días. Por eso Ramos estaba bateando en su lugar.
El entrenador Aaron Boone describió la noche como una oportunidad perdida, no como un partido robado, y sus palabras reflejaban la importancia del momento en el calendario.
«Obviamente, muchas cosas buenas, pero no las suficientes», dijo Boone. «Ha sido un golpe duro, claro, cuando tenías la oportunidad de barrer la serie y justo antes de un día de descanso. Pero tenemos que superarlo y prepararnos para enfrentarnos a un buen equipo de los Diamondbacks».
Al final del partido, Boone no se anduvo con rodeos con Lombard, pero tampoco lo machacó.
Boone reconoció que la bola de Caratini rebotó en el montículo, pero fue una jugada que Lombard «se espera que haga y sabemos que es capaz de hacer».
Rodón lo da todo en octubre, pero no saca nada a cambio
Carlos Rodón le dio a los Yankees el comienzo que necesita una rotación en la postemporada y vio cómo se esfumaba. El zurdo encajó dos carreras en seis entradas, ampliando su récord de la franquicia a 25 salidas consecutivas en las que ha encajado tres carreras o menos. Lanzó 102 lanzamientos, su máximo de la temporada, y bajó su promedio de carreras limpias a 2,95.
«Empecé un poco lento, un poco tenso», dijo Rodon. «Me fui soltando en las siguientes entradas, así que eso estuvo bien».
Clarke Schmidt hizo su tan esperado regreso en la séptima entrada, ponchando a dos antes de que Brent Headrick dejara a dos en base. El bullpen corrió una maratón que la alineación nunca supo recompensar.
Una primicia para el club que no se veía desde 1991
Este es el dato que pocos destacarán. Ha sido la primera derrota de los Yankees tras ir ganando varias veces en entradas extras desde el 5 de mayo de 1991, en Seattle, es decir, en un lapso de más de 34 años. También fue su octava derrota en la última entrada de la temporada, un récord de la franquicia, y ningún equipo de la MLB ha encajado más hits decisivos en la última entrada en 2026, según datos de Baseball Reference. Ningún equipo de los Yankees ha perdido nunca más partidos a domicilio en entradas extras en una sola temporada.
Lo curioso es que los equipos malos no acumulan cifras como estas. Un equipo mediocre pierde en nueve partidos. Solo un buen equipo es capaz de forzar una prórroga fuera de casa una y otra vez, y luego seguir perdiéndola.
Cómo queda la carrera por la División Este de la Liga Americana
Spencer Jones lanzó su propia advertencia, ponchándose cinco veces en una noche en la que se fue de 0 de 6, lo que demostró lo rápido que se castigan los swings fallidos cuando los márgenes se estrechan. En septiembre se lee de otra manera que en julio.
Los Yankees tienen el jueves libre antes de empezar una serie de fin de semana en Arizona, donde Gerrit Cole será el lanzador titular el viernes a las 21:40 h (hora del Este). No se espera que Judge tenga que hacerse más pruebas. Nueva York ha perdido terreno que quizá no recupere y le ha dado un respiro a los Rays.
Los Yankees saben cómo ganar los partidos intermedios. Una noche en la que solo tenían que ganar uno, no pudieron.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario aquí abajo.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Heliot Ramos Is Flying Under the Radar Down the Stretch for Yankees
item.dc:creator: Joe Najarian; Unknown
item.description: When Aaron Judge made his long-awaited return from the injured list last week, the New York Yankees subsequently reduced the playing time of fellow outfielder Heliot Ramos. This was always the plan, as the Yankees acquired Ramos at the trade deadline to be a platoon bat against left-handed pitching. item.content:encoded:
When Aaron Judge made his long-awaited return from the injured list last week, the New York Yankees subsequently reduced the playing time of fellow outfielder Heliot Ramos.
This was always the plan, as the Yankees acquired Ramos at the trade deadline to be a platoon bat against left-handed pitching. The 27-year-old's miserable start to his Bronx tenure as a starting outfielder not only cemented his bench role but also quickly made fans believe that trading for him was a huge mistake.
However, Ramos is sneakily turning things around since going to the bench, which is good, as Judge exited Wednesday's game with right lower-leg tightness. He's taking full advantage of the more sporadic at-bats he gets, driving the ball with authority and seeing results.
Heliot Ramos is figuring things out at the plate
It is worth mentioning that the game that got Ramos going came before Judge returned to the lineup and pushed him to the bench. On August 30 against the Boston Red Sox, the righty-swinging outfielder reached base in all four of his plate appearances and hit his first home run as a Yankee, a three-run shot that broke the game open.
Even then, Ramos failed to reach base in his next two games before going 1-for-2 with a single and a walk against the San Diego Padres on September 5, the last game he played before Judge was activated. But on September 8, Ramos pinch-hit for Judge in the eighth inning against the Colorado Rockies and promptly hit another three-run homer to seal another Yankee victory.
Ramos has since started two games in right field to give Judge a breather: those coming on September 12 against the New York Mets and on Tuesday night against the Minnesota Twins. Far more noteworthy was the Twins game, which saw Judge get the day off entirely.
Ramos was a key component to New York's production by going 2-for-4 with a walk, an RBI, and two runs scored; his third-inning walk allowed him to eventually score a two-out run, and he lashed an RBI double in the sixth inning that also set up a game-breaking homer by Spencer Jones shortly afterwards.
Dating back to Ramos' big day against Boston, he is slashing .350/.458/.700 in 24 plate appearances with a pair of homers, seven RBI and a 221 wRC+. Since Judge returned, Ramos has made only 11 plate appearances, but collected four hits (two for extra bases) and a walk with four RBI and three runs scored.
Even when Ramos was stuck in his terrible slump that lasted for most of August, most of the balls he put in play were hit very hard. 55.3% of Ramos' batted balls had an exit velocity of 95 mph or higher despite his miserable .119 batting average from August 4 to August 29. Ramos continues to make hard contact during his recent hot streak, with a 57.1% hard-hit rate, and the expected stats are not much lower than the actual stats (.473 xwOBA against a .488 wOBA).
Of course, the sample size is very small, and Ramos hasn't been productive in every single plate appearance. But it's still very encouraging to see him find results and come through with timely hits. As a bench player, the Yankees may rely on him even more to come through in clutch situations down the stretch, and they'd feel more comfortable putting the bat in Ramos' hands if he continues to hit.
*stats updated before Wednesday's game against the Twins
Joe Najarian is the Deputy Editor and a writer for the New York Yankees and New York Mets On SI sites. He got his bachelor’s degree in journalism with a specialization in sports from Rutgers University, graduating in 2022. Joe has previously written for Jersey Sporting News and for the New York Giants On SI site. You can follow him on Twitter/X: @JoeNajarian
Follow joenajarian

item.content:encoded:
Yahoo Sports: As you likely know by now, Aaron Judge exited yesterday's game early when Heliot Ramos pinch-hit for him in the sixth. The Yankees announced it midgame as "lower leg tightness." It's some relief I suppose that Judge didn't re-aggravate the rib fracture that kept him out for over three months, and Judge himself downplayed the seriousness of the ailment after the game.
"We're still trying to ramp up so there's still going to be little things like this that come up," Judge said after the Yankees 13-inning loss to the Twins. "I just thought it would be best instead of pushing through it like I normally do." Judge seemed to view his exit from the game as precautionary, and likened it to the type of thing that would happen in spring training when small, nagging things pop up as players get back into playing shape.
MLB.com | Patrick Donnelly: Clarke Schmidt came off the 60-day injured list yesterday, something we saw coming; he allowed two hits but got two strikeouts while facing four batters in his first MLB action since July 3, 2025. What we didn't see coming was who was pushed off the roster to make room for Schmidt: fan favorite Oswaldo Cabrera. The utilityman Cabrera had spent most of the year at Triple-A, hitting .288 with 19 homers and a .790 OPS, but hasn't spent much time with the big club ever since suffering a brutal ankle injury in a play at home plate last May. Cabrera seems likely to be claimed on waivers, meaning his time in the Bronx is likely to come to an end after being a member of the organization since signing at age-16 in July 2015.
The Athletic | Brendan Kuty: ($) Spencer Jones has been a bit of a revelation for the Yankees this year, producing at a high level across the outfield throughout the summer. He's benefited from shadowing another big lefty swinger in the outfield: Cody Bellinger. Bellinger is only 31, but has a very long and decorated track record for a player his age, something Jones has tried to tap into during his time with the Yankees. "As a young guy, I can't help but watch every time he's up there," Jones said of Bellinger. "When we are in the dugout," Jones said, "he's one of those people I can go up to and ask, like, 'Yo, what did you see?' He'll tell me bluntly what he saw, how he saw it, and essentially what he's going to do next time."
New York Daily News | Gary Phillips: Ryan Weathers cleared a key hurdle in his rehab earlier this week, tossing 15 pitches in a bullpen session and sitting 87-90 mph on his fastball. The hope, if things go right, is for the lefty to get into game action before the regular season ends. It's a tight timeline, but with Weathers set to throw another bullpen on Friday before perhaps facing live hitters early next week, it's doable. The Yankees could certainly use his arm in the bullpen as they try to sort out what their playoff relief corps will look like.
FanGraphs | Davy Andrews: This here isn't news, but it is fun. Andrews discusses the Amazon TV show Reacher, in which the titular character tries to maintain a low profile by checking into hotels under aliases, which are always Yankees second basemen. The problem, of course, is that Reacher's cover is often blown, because Yankee second basemen are frequently famous people with recognizable names (don't choose "Starlin Castro" as your alias if you're trying not to attract attention!). So, Andrews endeavors to help Reacher by finding players who played second base for the Yankees who would help Reacher stay undercover. Good aliases include second basemen from New York's Higlander days, like Joe Ward, and Otis Johnson. The worst possible aliases Andrews found? Robinson Canó and Mickey Mantle.

item.title: [nytimes.com] Yankees mailbag: Aaron Judge’s injury, Jasson Domínguez’s future and the playoff rotation
item.dc:creator: Chris Kirschner
item.description: The New York Yankees are now in wait-and-see mode. Aaron Judge left Wednesday’s game early with right leg tightness. There’s no word yet on whether he’ll have to miss time, and we likely won’t have an answer until Friday at the earliest. Before then, let’s answer some of your Yankees questions in part one of our mailbag. If you want to ask anything else, there’s still time to do so here. Note: Questions have been edited for clarity and brevity. Advertisement Assuming Trent Grisham is healthy, wh
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are now in wait-and-see mode.
Aaron Judge left Wednesday’s game early with right leg tightness. There’s no word yet on whether he’ll have to miss time, and we likely won’t have an answer until Friday at the earliest.
Before then, let’s answer some of your Yankees questions in part one of our mailbag. If you want to ask anything else, there’s still time to do so here.
Note: Questions have been edited for clarity and brevity.
Advertisement
Assuming Trent Grisham is healthy, who starts in center field during the playoffs: him or Spencer Jones? — Ed H.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone told reporters Wednesday that Grisham is running “up to a decent speed” in his comeback from a right hamstring strain. Considering Grisham at normal speed is slow, it’s anyone’s guess what that actually means.
If Grisham is ready to go, it will be interesting to see what Boone decides. There are numerous examples of the Yankees opting for the veteran over an inexperienced player like Jones when the games matter most.
Both players have their warts. Neither Grisham nor Jones is a good defensive center fielder. Jones looked abysmal in center, letting a ground ball go under his glove, dropping a fly ball that hit his glove and nearly trucking Heliot Ramos in right field. Meanwhile, Grisham has trouble getting to balls over his head and in the gaps because he’s slow-footed. There’s likely a higher floor of success, though, for Grisham. Even on the balls Jones has caught, there have been instances where he doesn’t look comfortable reading the play off the bat.
So the main difference will come down to offense.
Before Grisham injured his hamstring, he was not hitting. Calls for Jones to take over were already happening. To Jones’ credit, he has produced at the plate. Even after a dreadful 0-for-6 performance with five strikeouts on Wednesday, Jones has a 113 wRC+. He is always a threat to pop a home run, and that wins ballgames in October.
Grisham has one of the best eyes on the team, rarely strikes out and works at-bats. That matters when the batters behind him would likely be Ben Rice and Judge (depending on his health).
Not that my opinion holds any weight, but I’d stick with Jones in center field. The Yankees can always use Grisham, who’s one of the most clutch hitters on the team, in big spots off the bench.
Advertisement
What will/should the Yankees playoff rotation and bullpen look like? I hate to say it, but Gerrit Cole and Max Fried are not looking like aces these days. The team is winning Will Warren’s and Carlos Rodón’s starts. How are these facts likely to influence Boone’s postseason rotation decisions? … As soon as I say this, Fried pitches a gem. Jinx. — Aaron D.
The American League East race isn’t over yet, but the likeliest outcome is the Yankees will play in a wild-card series against the Boston Red Sox. That means the Yankees will only need three starting pitchers for the first round.
Cam Schlittler should start Game 1. There’s no argument otherwise. Schlittler is one of the very best starting pitchers in the sport. You want your best pitcher going in Game 1 to give yourself the best possible chance of not facing a must-win Game 2.
From there, it’ll be a toss-up between Fried and Cole. Both pitchers have concerns attached to them.
Fried has battled command issues all season, while Cole has allowed plenty of hard contact while not getting much swing-and-miss. I’d lean toward Fried over Cole.
As for the bullpen, the Yankees could have Rodón in case the club needs length. The others likely to be on the roster are Will Warren, David Bednar, Brent Headrick, Paul Blackburn, John Schreiber, Clarke Schmidt, Ryan Yarbrough and Ryan Weathers, if he’s healthy. I’d leave off Tim Hill, who has struggled mightily this season, Luis Gil and Michael Fulmer.
What is the realistic outlook for second base next year? Jazz Chisholm Jr. hasn’t played up to his talent, which might make him more enticing by bringing down his cost. The infield is already crowded, though, with Ryan McMahon under contract, George Lombard Jr.’s promotion, José Caballero, two first basemen (three if Paul Goldschmidt is still seen as Giancarlo Stanton insurance), and Anthony Volpe’s re-ascension. — Marco F.
What the Yankees decide to do at second base is one of the most fascinating storylines of the offseason.
Advertisement
I agree with you, Marco, that this season has likely cost Chisholm millions. He is nearing the end of his worst offensive season since 2021. He won’t reach the heights he set for himself entering 2026, but he still could reach a 20-40 season. Few players have the talent to post those numbers. Before this year, Chisholm posted back-to-back 4+ fWAR seasons. It would not be wrong for the Yankees or another team to bet on his upside.
Chisholm still offers tremendous defense at second and excellent baserunning. If his bat gets back to being considerably above average, he profiles as one of the best second basemen in the sport. There are valid concerns about his offense, though. His hit tool is considerably below average, and as he ages and loses athleticism, that could be a major problem that he cannot overcome.
The Yankees should consider giving Chisholm a short-term deal, though. He is a better option than Caballero and Volpe, who are better as role players, and few available players are better than what he can provide.
The Yankees should strongly consider playing Caballero or Volpe, who played a few games in the minors there, at third base. McMahon is one of the worst everyday regulars in the big leagues this season, and there’s a higher likelihood of Caballero or Volpe producing at the plate.
Has the Martian played his last game in a Yankees uniform? — oconnell13
It’s a hard question to answer because you can’t predict injuries. You never know if the Yankees will have to reach into the minor leagues for depth.
But it’s not far-fetched to think Jasson Domínguez will never play in another important game for the Yankees again. He cannot be trusted in the field. Every game matters for the Yankees, and there’s always a queasy feeling when the ball is hit his way.
His bat also hasn’t progressed enough to keep giving him chances to prove himself. Jones has leapfrogged him on the depth chart, and the Yankees now have Heliot Ramos on their roster. There may not be space for Domínguez.
Advertisement
What are the Yankees’ pitching plans for the rest of the regular season? Specifically, who’s lining up for the Rays series and will any of them be limited in terms of pitch count? — Nick B.
As of now, the Yankees are lined up to start their best four starters against the Rays next week. Here’s how it looks:
Tuesday: Fried and Rodón are in line to start the games of the doubleheader.
Wednesday: Cole
Thursday: Schlittler
The Rays are also on track to start their best pitchers for that series. They could start Nick Martinez and Drew Rasmussen on Tuesday, Freddy Peralta on Wednesday and Ian Seymour on Thursday. Their rotation is dependent on what they decide to do for their weekend series against the Boston Red Sox. But if they wanted, all of these pitchers could factor into their pitching plans next week.
Any chance the Yanks consider Ben Rice as the backup catcher on the postseason roster to free up an extra bench spot for someone more versatile (and better than) Ali Sánchez/J.C. Escarra? — Matthew L.
The odds of this happening are close to zero.
Earlier in the season, Rice kept catching behind the scenes. Before games, he’d catch bullpens and do on-field drills with director of catching Tanner Swanson. Rice hasn’t done any of that in months.
If anything, Rice would only be used in an emergency situation. Believe it or not, the organization believes in Sánchez. That’s why they didn’t promote Mitch Garver. Sánchez is out of minor league options, so they’d have to designate him for assignment and risk him getting claimed off waivers. They value the consistency he provides to their pitchers, and they think he’s a better defender than the metrics show.

item.title: [Claro Sports] Aaron Judge preocupa a los Yankees: sale del partido por una molestia en la pantorrilla derecha
item.dc:creator: Gael Gonzalez Flores
item.description: Los Bombarderos del Bronx esperan la recuperación de su capitán para disputar los playoffs de la MLB La preocupación volvió a aparecer alrededor de Aaron Judge, quien tuvo que abandonar el encuentro entre los New York Yankees y Minnesota Twins debido a una molestia en la parte inferior de la pierna derecha. El jardinero derecho salió del partido durante la sexta entrada de la derrota de Nueva York por 5-4 en extra innings. El capitán de los Yankees fue reemplazado por Heliot Ramos como bateador
item.content:encoded:
Los Bombarderos del Bronx esperan la recuperación de su capitán para disputar los playoffs de la MLB
La preocupación volvió a aparecer alrededor de Aaron Judge, quien tuvo que abandonar el encuentro entre los New York Yankees y Minnesota Twins debido a una molestia en la parte inferior de la pierna derecha. El jardinero derecho salió del partido durante la sexta entrada de la derrota de Nueva York por 5-4 en extra innings.
El capitán de los Yankees fue reemplazado por Heliot Ramos como bateador emergente, después de que en sus dos turnos al bate ante el lanzador Zebby Matthews se fue ponchado. Judge había descansado el martes como parte de la programación del equipo, pero esta vez tuvo que dejar el terreno por precaución.
La molestia apareció durante el desarrollo del partido, aunque Judge no mostró señales evidentes de dolor durante sus acciones defensivas. En la quinta entrada, el pelotero corrió hacia la zona entre los jardines para perseguir un doblete, en la que fue su última participación antes de salir del encuentro.
MÁS INFORMACIÓN: Brewers conquistan por cuarto año consecutivo la División Central de la Liga Nacional
Aaron Judge explica la decisión de abandonar el juego
Después del partido, Aaron Judge explicó que sintió rigidez en la zona afectada desde la primera entrada, pero intentó continuar debido a la importancia de los últimos juegos de la temporada regular.
“Intenté restarle importancia y ver cuánto podía aguantar, ya que estos juegos son importantes en la recta final de la temporada”, señaló Judge. Sin embargo, después de hablarlo con el cuerpo técnico, consideró que lo mejor era abandonar el partido para evitar una situación que pudiera afectar al equipo.
El tres veces ganador del Jugador Más Valioso de la Liga Americana explicó que la decisión tuvo como objetivo no arriesgar una lesión mayor y permitir que otro jugador pudiera ocupar su lugar. “Pensé que lo correcto era salir del juego para no perjudicar al equipo, ya fuera en el campo o en las bases”, comentó el bateador de los Yankees.
Judge también señaló que este tipo de molestias pueden aparecer durante el proceso de recuperación y aumento de intensidad después de una ausencia prolongada. “Van a surgir pequeños inconvenientes como éste. Simplemente pensé que era mejor no forzar la situación”, agregó.
Aaron Boone confirma contractura en la pantorrilla derecha
El manager de los Yankees, Aaron Boone, confirmó que la molestia de Judge corresponde a una contractura en la parte inferior de la pierna derecha, específicamente en la pantorrilla.
El estratega explicó que el pelotero comenzó a sentir la rigidez después de uno de sus turnos al bate y que, tras consultar con el cuerpo médico, se tomó la decisión de retirarlo del partido como medida preventiva.
“Ya ha recibido bastante terapia en la zona tras salir del juego. Mañana jueves continuará bajo estricto tratamiento médico y ahí evaluaremos qué es lo que realmente tenemos”, explicó Boone.
Una de las principales preocupaciones dentro de la organización era conocer si la molestia estaba relacionada con la lesión que mantuvo fuera de actividad a Judge durante varios meses. Sin embargo, Boone aclaró que esta situación no tiene relación con la fractura por estrés en la costilla que sufrió anteriormente.
Yankees esperan contar con Judge para la postemporada
La salida de Judge llega en un momento importante para los Yankees, que ya aseguraron su lugar en la postemporada y se encuentran en la pelea por mejorar su posición dentro de la Liga Americana.
Desde su regreso tras la ausencia por la fractura de costilla, Judge batea de 26-4 con 13 ponches y un extrabase en siete partidos. Además, conectó un cuadrangular durante el primer juego de la serie ante Minnesota, el mismo día en que Nueva York confirmó su clasificación a los playoffs.
Aaron Boone destacó la importancia del jardinero dentro del equipo y aseguró que esperan que pueda recuperarse para ser una pieza importante en octubre. “Obviamente, él es una pieza clave en lo que hacemos. Esperamos tratar la molestia, superarla y que él pueda ser un factor importante en algún momento”, indicó el manager.
Los Yankees tendrán descanso este jueves antes de iniciar una serie como visitantes ante los Arizona Diamondbacks, una ventana que el equipo aprovechará para evaluar la evolución de Judge y determinar los siguientes pasos en su recuperación.

item.content:encoded:
On Wednesday, the New York Yankees and Minnesota Twins finished their series at Target Field.
The Yankees were unable to complete the sweep, as they lost by a score of 5-4 (in 13 innings).
One of the biggest moments in the game came when Heliot Ramos grounded into a double-play with the bases loaded (and no one out) in the 12th inning.
Yankees Trade Looking Worse By The Day
Ramos (who was an All-Star in 2024) was traded to the Yankees via the San Francisco Giants earlier this year.
While he has played better as of late, the trade has not worked out so far.
The Yankees wrote (via X) on August 3: “The New York Yankees today announced that they have acquired outfielder Heliot Ramos from the San Francisco Giants in exchange for minor league infielder Kaeden Kent and left-handed pitcher Henry Lalane.
Social Media On Ramos
Here’s what people were saying on Wednesday:
@_cheeksii: “I’m done rooting for the Yankees solely because of Heliot Ramos”
@InvestSportsInc: “Wow Ramos is just horrendous. That was the ball game right there.”
@SavageNtheBox: “Bro, bases loaded and no outs and Heliot Ramos did the absolute worst worst thing you can do in that situation. Literally cant make it up lmaooo”
@octoberstanton: “This can’t happen in a playoff race”
@JLas43_: “Ramos vs RHP is a bad matchup
@ShaunMorash: “Heliot Ramos with an all time disgrace of an at bat”
@Jwiesel13: “I would’ve rather had Judge wincing in pain at the plate than Ramos”
Looking At The Yankees Right Now
The Yankees are the second-place team in the American League East with an 88-64 record in 152 games.
They will now visit the Arizona Diamondbacks on Friday night in Phoenix.

item.title: [The Japan Times] Yankees slugger Aaron Judge exits game against Twins
item.dc:creator: Int-No Author
item.description: New York slugger Aaron Judge exited in the sixth inning of Wednesday’s game against the Minnesota Twins because of tightness in his lower right leg. Judge said he was injured during the first inning and later reported the ailment to manager Aaron Boone, who removed him from the game. “I tried to play it off and see how long we can go because these games are important down the stretch,” Judge said after a 5-4, 13-inning loss to the Twins. “But talking it over, I thought it would be the right move
item.content:encoded:
New York slugger Aaron Judge exited in the sixth inning of Wednesday’s game against the Minnesota Twins because of tightness in his lower right leg.
Judge said he was injured during the first inning and later reported the ailment to manager Aaron Boone, who removed him from the game.
“I tried to play it off and see how long we can go because these games are important down the stretch,” Judge said after a 5-4, 13-inning loss to the Twins. “But talking it over, I thought it would be the right move to come out so we don’t cost the team on the field or cost the team on the basepaths.”
Judge, 34, was playing in his seventh game since returning from a 99-day absence due to a stress fracture in his first right rib.
Boone said he was informed that Judge’s leg “just felt tight” after heading out to right field after batting in the first inning.
“He said he felt a little something after the first inning,” Boone said. “Hopefully it’s something we are able to catch.”
Judge was replaced by pinch hitter Heliot Ramos in the sixth with the Yankees trailing 2-0. Ramos also filled his position in right field.
The Yankees have an off day on Thursday before beginning a three-game series against the host Arizona Diamondbacks. But Judge didn’t think his injury would require any imaging. He said the situation is part of returning from a lengthy time away from the field.
“Once you start ramping up, things pop up,” Judge said. “Hopefully, it’s just one little thing and we’re back out there soon.”
Judge struck out in his two at-bats to lower his average this season to .241 in 66 games. The eight-time All-Star and three-time American League MVP (2022, 2024, 2025) has 18 home runs and 41 RBIs this season.
After missing 84 games since May 31, Judge was 3-for-17 (.176) with no extra-base hits in his first five games back from injury before hitting a three-run homer on Monday as New York clinched a postseason berth with an 8-3 victory over Minnesota.

item.content:encoded:
Yankees news: Spencer Jones joins Aaron Judge club nobody wants in loss to Twins appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
New York Yankees rookie Spencer Jones joined an unwanted club Wednesday, striking out five times in a 5-4, 13-inning loss to the Minnesota Twins at Target Field.
Jones went 0-for-6 as New York's starting center fielder, becoming the first Yankees hitter to strike out five times in a game since superstar Aaron Judge did so against the Pittsburgh Pirates on September 28, 2024. The outing marked Judge's third career five-strikeout game, while Jones recorded his first in the majors.
Talkin' Yanks noted the connection on X, formerly Twitter, one day after Jones hit a three-run homer in New York's 8-1 win.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
"Spencer Jones becomes the first Yankee to strikeout five times in one game since Aaron Judge in September of 2024"
Jones entered the game batting .259/.331/.452 with 10 home runs. His hitless afternoon dropped that line to .252/.323/.440, while his strikeout rate sits around 35 percent.
Twins starter Zebby Matthews held the Yankees to two hits across six scoreless innings while recording eight strikeouts. Carlos Rodon countered by allowing two runs on four hits across six innings for New York.
The Yankees did not score until Anthony Volpe delivered a two-out, two-run double in the ninth frame. Both teams scored in the 10th and 11th before going scoreless in the 12th. In the 13th, pinch hitter Victor Caratini singled home automatic runner Luke Keaschall to secure the walk-off victory for the Twins.
The Yankees tied a season high with 17 strikeouts and set another by stranding 13 runners. Their afternoon worsened in the sixth inning when Judge exited with lower right leg tightness after striking out in both at-bats. Heliot Ramos replaced him.
The loss dropped the Yankees to 88-64, four games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the American League East. The Twins improved to 71-81, avoided a sweep, and finished the six-game season series tied at three wins apiece. For Jones, the five-strikeout performance underscored the contact concerns surrounding the 6-foot-7 outfielder, whom New York selected 25th overall in 2022.
Related: Yankees' Aaron Judge shares his side of story about leg tightness concern
Related: Brutal George Lombard Jr. error results in walk-off Twins win vs. Yankees

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yankees Fans Breathe Sigh of Relief After Aaron Judge Injury Scare
item.dc:creator: Pat Pickens
item.description: Captain Aaron Judge exited the New York Yankees' game against the Minnesota Twins on Wednesday with right-leg tightness. Outfielder Heliot Ramos pinch hit for Judge during his spot in the sixth inning. Judge was 0-for-2 with a pair of strikeouts. The Yankees did not initially provide any update the injury, leaving fans to speculate the worst for nearly an hour before YES' Meredith Markaovits reported the leg prognosis. Judge missed 84 games with a stress fracture in his right rib, and the Yankee
item.content:encoded:
Captain Aaron Judge exited the New York Yankees' game against the Minnesota Twins on Wednesday with right-leg tightness.
Outfielder Heliot Ramos pinch hit for Judge during his spot in the sixth inning. Judge was 0-for-2 with a pair of strikeouts.
The Yankees did not initially provide any update the injury, leaving fans to speculate the worst for nearly an hour before YES' Meredith Markaovits reported the leg prognosis.
Judge missed 84 games with a stress fracture in his right rib, and the Yankees were one of the worst offensive teams in baseball in that span.
Judge returned Sept. 8 against the Colorado Rockies — he left that game early too — and hit his first home run since coming back from the injury in the Yankees' 8-3 win over the Twins that clinched a playoff berth Monday.
The Yankees captain got the day off Tuesday, and the Yankees are off Thursday before their three-game weekend series against the Arizona Diamondbacks.
Judge is slashing .241/.360/.511 with 18 home runs and 41 RBIs through 66 games.
Aaron Judge Left Wednesday's Yankees Game in the Sixth Inning
YES Network cameras captured Judge appearing to grimace during a check swing in his final at-bat. He remained in the game, struck out again in the third inning to strand two runners then fielded Ben Ross' double off the wall in the fifth inning.
But all of Yankees Universe held its breath when Ramos stepped up to the plate in Judge's spot for the sixth inning, especially after YES Network analyst and Judge's former manager, Joe Girardi, said what Yankees fans were thinking.
"Something has to be up," Girardi said.
Ramos, whom the Yankees acquired from the San Francisco Giants before the trade deadline as insurance for Judge, struck out in his at-bat. He took over in right field in the bottom of the sixth inning.
The Yankees Can't Afford to Lose Aaron Judge
The Yankees were being shut out when Judge exited the game Wednesday, held in check by Twins starter Zebby Matthews.
But you can feel the sigh of relief from Yankees fans after Marakovits' reporting.
The Yankees offense was again beginning to find its footing with Judge back. They ranked tied for 26th in the majors in runs, 26th in slugging percentage (.386) and dead last in on-base percentage (.295) over the three-plus months Judge was out of the lineup.
Judge's postseason struggles are well-documented, but the Yankees really can't afford not to have him in their lineup when the calendar flips to October with any injury.
Aside from being a three-time American League MVP, Judge also balances out the Yankees' left-hand-heavy lineup, joining infielders Anthony Volpe and George Lombard Jr. as the only righties in their regular starting nine.
A second straight wild-card-round date with the Boston Red Sox, and their co-ace lefties Garrett Crochet and Payton Tolle, is looming. The Yankees are already likely to be without Giancarlo Stanton and not having Judge would be even more problematic.
Like HEAVY's content? Be sure to follow us.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Yankees Fans Breathe Sigh of Relief After Aaron Judge Injury Scare appeared first on HEAVY.

item.title: [The New York Times] Aaron Judge exits Yankees game with leg injury: ‘We’re still trying to ramp up’
item.dc:creator: Brendan Kuty
item.description: MINNEAPOLIS — There was still a mystery surrounding the injury that forced New York Yankees star Aaron Judge to want to leave the game in the sixth inning of a 5-4, 13-inning loss to the Minnesota Twins on Wednesday. item.content:encoded:
MINNEAPOLIS — There was still a mystery surrounding the injury that forced New York Yankees star Aaron Judge to want to leave the game in the sixth inning of a 5-4, 13-inning loss to the Minnesota Twins on Wednesday.
The Yankees said Judge was dealing with right lower leg tightness, but Judge refused to confirm which leg was troubling him, let alone which part. Instead, Judge said he was dealing with something in his “lower body.”
When asked whether he would go for tests, he said “probably not,” but also, “I have no idea.”
Was Judge concerned? He didn’t say.
Advertisement
“We’re still trying to ramp up,” he said. “So there’s going to be little things like this as they come up. Just thought it would be best (to leave the game) instead of pushing through like I normally do, and it might become a little worse. Get somebody who’s ready to go in there. Trying to do what’s best for the team.”
Judge appeared to limp a little in right field at points during the game. Manager Aaron Boone said the 34-year-old felt discomfort after the first inning, but that he wasn’t told Judge was dealing with anything until just before he took him out of the game.
“He said he felt a little something after the first inning and whenever it was I took him out,” Boone said. “That’s when I was made aware of it and just didn’t want to push through anything, and hopefully it’s something we’re able to catch.”
Judge likened it to an injury “you deal with this every spring training.”
“At the start of the season, once you start ramping up again, things pop up,” he said. “That’s where we’ve been, thankfully, this whole time coming back. Nothing’s really nagged us. Hope this is just one little thing and we’re back out there soon.”
Judge left Wednesday’s game before his at-bat in the sixth inning with a runner on first base, one out and the Yankees trailing 2-0. Heliot Ramos took over for Judge. Judge was 0-for-2 with two swinging strikeouts before exiting. He had Tuesday off.
The Yankees are off Thursday. They play three games on turf at Chase Field against the Arizona Diamondbacks starting Friday.
His early exit is likely worrisome to Yankees fans, who waited more than three months for his return from a stress fracture in his first right rib. He rejoined the lineup Sept. 8. That day, Boone removed him after six innings, and Judge said he was “not happy” about the decision, wanting to play a full nine innings despite having not played since May 31.
Advertisement
Judge declined to take a rehab assignment before returning from his rib injury. Instead, he took a round of live batting practice, hit off a high-velocity pitching machine and had a coach hit fly balls to him.
Since returning, he is just 4-for-23 (.173), with his sole home run coming Monday, helping the Yankees clinch an American League playoff spot.
The Yankees have 10 regular-season games remaining, and they are four games behind the AL East division-leading Tampa Bay Rays, whom they host for a four-game set next week.
“I kind of tried to play it off and see how we go because these games are important down the stretch,” he said. “Kind of talked it over, thought it would be the right move to come out so we don’t cost the team in the field or cost the team on the base paths.”

item.content:encoded:
MINNEAPOLIS -- Los primeros dos juegos de la serie de esta semana en el Target Field no pudieron haber salido mucho mejor para los Yankees. Ganaron ambos con comodidad, y el lunes Aaron Judge conectó su primer jonrón desde que regresó de la lista de lesionados el 8 de septiembre.
Pero no se puede culpar a los fans de los Yankees por preocuparse luego de que Judge fuera reemplazado por un bateador emergente en la sexta entrada del partido del miércoles, que al final los Bombarderos perdieron por 5-4 en 13 entradas. El club anunció más tarde que el cañonero fue retirado debido a rigidez en la parte inferior de la pierna derecha.
Judge, quien descansó en el encuentro del martes como parte de un día libre de rutina tras disputar seis choques consecutivos, se ponchó en cada uno de sus primeros dos turnos ante el abridor de los Mellizos, Zebby Matthews, el miércoles. Las imágenes de video parecieron mostrar a Judge haciendo una mueca de dolor durante uno de sus swings.
El boricua Heliot Ramos bateó de emergente por Judge y también se ponchó ante Matthews, quien abanicó a ocho rivales en 6.0 capítulos en blanco.

item.title: [marca usa] Aaron Judge desata la preocupación tras abandonar el juego por una lesión repentina días después de volver a MLB
item.dc:creator: Jose Rodriguez
item.description: Los New York Yankees ya aseguraron su lugar en los playoffs y mantienen el objetivo de conquistar otra Serie Mundial, pero este miércoles surgió una nueva preocupación alrededor de su máxima figura: Aaron Judge. El capitán de los Yankees, quien apenas había regresado la semana pasada de la lista de lesionados, tuvo que abandonar el partido ante los Minnesota Twins, generando incertidumbre dentro de la organización y entre sus aficionados. ACTUALIZACIÓN: La salida de Judge se debió a una “rigidez
item.content:encoded:
Los New York Yankees ya aseguraron su lugar en los playoffs y mantienen el objetivo de conquistar otra Serie Mundial, pero este miércoles surgió una nueva preocupación alrededor de su máxima figura: Aaron Judge.
El capitán de los Yankees, quien apenas había regresado la semana pasada de la lista de lesionados, tuvo que abandonar el partido ante los Minnesota Twins, generando incertidumbre dentro de la organización y entre sus aficionados.
ACTUALIZACIÓN: La salida de Judge se debió a una “rigidez en la parte baja de la pierna derecha”, de acuerdo con Meredith Marakovits, reportera de YES Network.
El motivo de su salida temprana no había sido confirmado inicialmente. Brendan Kuty, periodista de The Athletic, informó que el jardinero fue retirado del encuentro antes de que terminara, aunque también dejó abierta la posibilidad de que se tratara de una decisión planeada de descanso.
“Judge salió temprano del juego. No estoy seguro de qué se trata. Pero todos nos volvemos locos con estas situaciones; existe la posibilidad de que Boone le estuviera dando medio partido antes del vuelo a Arizona y el día libre de mañana. A los Yankees les gusta hacer mucho eso de un ‘día de descanso antes del día libre’, y quizá esto sea una versión de eso”, escribió Kuty en X, antes Twitter.
“Por otro lado, él tuvo descanso ayer. Y están saltándose el turno al bate de Judge cuando podrían haberle permitido tomarlo y después retirarlo. Quién sabe”, agregó el periodista.
Sin embargo, la situación llamó la atención debido a que Judge ya había descansado en el partido anterior y Nueva York decidió no darle otro turno al bate antes de sacarlo del encuentro.
Aaron Judge apenas regresaba de una larga ausencia
El momento en el que llegó la molestia aumentó la preocupación. Judge se perdió más de tres meses de la temporada debido a una lesión en las costillas y apenas fue activado de la lista de lesionados de 60 días la semana pasada.
El toletero abandonó el encuentro en la sexta entrada, cuando Heliot Ramos ingresó como bateador emergente en su lugar. Durante la transmisión, el exmanager de los Yankees y actual analista Joe Girardi señaló que “debe haber algún problema” para que el equipo tomara esa decisión.
Los Yankees esperan que la situación no sea grave, especialmente con la postemporada cada vez más cerca. La salud de Judge será una de las principales historias de Nueva York mientras la franquicia continúa en busca de otro campeonato.

item.title: [MLB.com] Yankees to see how Judge (lower leg tightness) recovers after early exit in 13-inning loss

item.content:encoded:
MINNEAPOLIS -- The first two games of this week’s series at Target Field couldn’t have gone much better for the Yankees. They won both handily, and on Monday Aaron Judge hit his first home run since returning from the IL on Sept. 8.
Judge, who sat out Tuesday’s game as a routine day off after playing six straight games, struck out in each of his first two at-bats against Twins starter Zebby Matthews on Wednesday. After the game, he said he felt a stiffness in his lower right leg in the first inning.
“I tried to kind of play it off and see how long we could go, because these games are important down the stretch,” Judge said. “But kind of talking it over, I thought it'd be the right move to come out, so I don't cost the team on the field or cost the team on the basepath.”
With an off-day scheduled for Thursday, the team will wait to issue any prognosis on the severity of the injury until after he’s received extensive treatment over the next 48 hours.
“We’re not going to speculate one way or the other. We’ll just see how he responds,” manager Aaron Boone said.
Judge, who said he didn’t anticipate getting testing done, said he couldn’t pinpoint any specific activity or movement that triggered the stiffness, but the feeling isn’t an unfamiliar one to him.
“I feel like you deal with this every Spring Training. You know, usually at the start of the season once you start ramping up again, things pop up, and that's where we've been,” Judge said. “Thankfully, this whole time coming back, nothing's really nagged us. So hopefully it's just one little thing and then we're back out there soon.”
It would be a huge blow to the team to lose Judge after just getting him back into the lineup for the first time in three months. But at the same time, professional athletes and their coaches have to keep an eye on the big picture, and one Wednesday afternoon game against the Twins in mid-September pales in importance compared to upcoming series against the Diamondbacks, Rays and Orioles, plus whatever postseason action the team might see.
That’s especially true when that four-game series against Tampa Bay starting Tuesday could still determine the AL East champions -- and potentially a first-round bye in the postseason.
“Obviously he’s a key figure of what we do,” Boone said. “Hopefully we get it treated and knock it out and be a factor at some point.”
Heliot Ramos pinch-hit for Judge and also struck out against Matthews, who fanned eight in six scoreless innings. Ramos would likely fill in for Judge in right field during any absence he might incur.
The Yankees certainly could have used Judge’s bat in the lineup as they traded blows with the Twins in extra innings, after Anthony Volpe smacked a game-tying double off the wall in the top of the ninth with his club down to its final out.
In the 12th, the Yanks squandered an opportunity with the bases loaded and nobody out, as Ramos grounded into a double play, with Volpe thrown out at home plate. Ali Sánchez then struck out to end the threat, before Twins pinch-hitter Victor Caratini delivered a walk-off single up the middle in the 13th.

He said he felt a little something after the first inning, and whenever it was I took him out
item.content:encoded:
New York Yankees star Aaron Judge exited Wednesday’s 5-4 loss to the Minnesota Twins at Target Field in the sixth inning with right lower leg tightness, according to multiple reports.
Following Wednesday’s game, Yankees manager Aaron Boone was asked about Judge’s injury.
New York Yankees’ Aaron Boone Makes Aaron Judge Statement Amid Injury News
“I was made aware of [the injury] right before he came out. He said he felt a little something after the first inning, and whenever it was I took him out, that’s when I was made aware of it, and I just didn’t want to push through anything. Hopefully it’s something we’re able to catch.”
Boone said he doesn’t know if Judge will have to miss games.
Looking at Aaron Judge
Judge started Wednesday’s game as the right fielder. The outfielder hit third in the lineup before being replaced by Heliot Ramos in the sixth inning.
Judge went 0-for-2 with two strikeouts in Wednesday’s game.
Aaron Judge missed most the season with a right rib stress fracture. New York placed him on the IL on June 2. He didn’t return until Sept. 7.
Judge has struggled since returning from the IL, hitting just .190/.227/.333 with one home run and three RBI over six games.
Before being placed on the IL, Judge hit .248/.375/.533 with 17 home runs and 38 RBI over 59 games this season.
Since making his MLB debut in 2016, Judge has slashed .291/.410/.610 with 386 home runs and 871 RBI. He has won three AL MVP Awards.
New York Yankees Right Now
The Yankees won the first two games of their series against the Twins before losing the finale 5-4 in extra innings on Wednesday.
The Yankees’ record dropped to 88-64 after the loss. New York is now four-games behind the Tampa Bay Rays for first place in the American League East. The club has a 5 1/2-game lead over the Boston Red Sox for the first AL Wild Card spot.
Next, the Yankees will begin a three-game series against the Arizona Diamondbacks in Phoenix on Friday after an off day on Thursday.

item.title: [amNewYork] Aaron Judge injury: Latest on Yankees slugger’s leg, more | amNewYork

item.content:encoded:
With the postseason less than two weeks away, the Yankees are left holding their breath regarding the status of their slugging captain, Aaron Judge, who left Wednesday’s game against the Minnesota Twins early with what the team described as right lower-leg tightness.
Judge, who started the game in right field, was seen wincing during his second and final at-bat of the afternoon in the top of the third inning following a check-swing. He was pinch-hit for by Heliot Ramos in the top of the sixth, sending up immediate red flags for a team fighting to catch the Tampa Bay Rays for the top spot in the American League East.
Manager Aaron Boone said that Juge felt something in the first inning and took him out to make sure he didn’t “push through anything.”
He will undergo treatment, and the team will get a better sense of how severe the issue is on Thursday.
There may be some relief in that it is not his rib or oblique that is bothering him, though such a statement is a bit premature, considering the specifics of this lower-leg issue is unknown. Judge has already missed three months this season due to a rib injury that kept him out from late May to Sept. 7.
Wednesday’s game was just his seventh game back from the injured list, and he has struggled mightily after the long layoff, going 4-for-23 (.173) with one home run, three RBI, and 13 strikeouts.
Boone previously stated that he was going to take things slow with Judge because they forewent a rehab assignment. But he played six straight games before getting Tuesday off — the day after New York clinched its ninth postseason berth in 10 years.
The prospect of being without Judge this postseason should be a daunting one for the Yankees. Their offense struggled mightily without him, scoring 341 runs in the 84 games without him (4.06 runs per game). Only the Cincinnati Reds, Toronto Blue Jays, Cleveland Guardians, Los Angeles Angels, and Seattle Mariners scored fewer runs in all of baseball during that stretch.
Still, the Bronx Bombers should like their chances regardless of the status of their captain. The American League is exceptionally poor this season, with only six teams possessing records over .500. Three of them, including the Yankees, inhabit the AL East.
They also have one of the most imposing pitching staffs in all of baseball, as they are set to trot out AL Cy Young favorite Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, and Carlos Rodon in a shortened postseason rotation.
